title: Random Controlled Differential Equations
one_liner: Train only a single linear layer atop a giant randomly frozen time model, avoiding the cost of updating millions of weights.
lead: Predicting future values in a time series (stock prices, weather, sensor readings) usually means training a huge model with millions of weight updates. This paper freezes a randomly built model and trains only one small linear layer on top, keeping it fast and simple while capturing complex temporal patterns through random features and differential equations.

problem.h2: Training large time models is slow
paras: Every time you train a sequence model (a neural network that processes a stream of numbers), you run gradient descent: compute an error, nudge each of millions of weights in the direction that shrinks it, repeat hundreds of times. This is expensive — it requires many forward and backward passes, and storing all the intermediate values in memory. For real-time applications or edge devices, you cannot afford this cost.

A beginner might try training a tiny model instead, but tiny models do not see enough past context to make good predictions. You need a model that remembers thousands of past values, but training it is prohibitively slow.

callout.b: The paper's move, in one sentence:
callout.html: Freeze a randomly initialized model and train only the final single linear layer that reads off the output, avoiding the cost of updating the frozen weights.

panels.title: 1. The cost: train every weight
panels.caption: Every weight needs gradient updates across many time steps.

panels.title: 2. Freeze the model randomly
panels.caption: Randomly initialize the model once; never change these weights again.

panels.title: 3. Random features lift the signal
panels.viz_args: Fourier waves transform the input into a richer space without training.
panels.caption: Apply random waves to the input before the frozen model.

panels.title: 4. Train only the readout
panels.caption: Train one small linear layer that reads the frozen model's output.

panels.title: 5. Fast, accurate predictions
panels.viz_args: Linear layer output: next value or classification.
panels.caption: Predictions are made in milliseconds without full model retraining.

steps.text: Create a controlled differential equation (a system that evolves continuously over time) with random weights, never changed.
Transform each input using random Fourier features (random waves at different frequencies and phases), creating a richer representation.

steps.b: Run inputs through the frozen model
steps.text: Feed the lifted inputs into the random differential equation, which evolves over time and outputs complex patterns.
Store all the values the frozen model produces across the time series.
Fit a single linear layer on top to predict the target (next value, classification, or other label) from the frozen representations.

paras: Instead of training a sequence model by updating all its weights, this paper trains only the final linear layer and leaves the internal model completely frozen.

hidden.name: path signature (higher-order temporal features)
paras: A path signature is a mathematical summary of a path (a stream of values over time) that captures not just the values themselves but the order and sequence of changes. It is similar to a fingerprint: two completely different time series can produce the same sequence of points, but the signature tells them apart because it records how the path moved through space.

This paper estimates the path signature implicitly: instead of computing it directly, the random differential equation model automatically produces features that span the space of all possible path signatures. The random features and the continuous-time dynamics together mean the frozen model outputs representations that encode these higher-order temporal patterns without explicit computation.

heat.caption: Darker means higher-order temporal feature. Marked cells show signature information the method implicitly captures.

reads.html: A path signature is what you get if you write down not just where a point went, but every way it wiggled getting there — all the curves, reversals, speeds. It is a complete record of the path's shape.

In the infinite-width limit, the random controlled differential equation approximates the rough signature transformation of the input path, capturing all higher-order terms without explicit computation.

mechanism.h2: Why freezing works: random features already capture what matters
paras: When you randomly initialize a large neural network and freeze it, the network's weights are a fixed 'basis' — like an unchangeable coordinate system. Adding more random features (sine waves at random frequencies) expands this basis, so the frozen network can express more patterns without ever changing its weights.

The reason this works for time series: random features at many different frequencies can approximate any smooth function of the input. The continuous-time differential equation (which evolves smoothly) then composes these features over time, automatically producing representations that encode the full history of the input path. Training only the readout layer finds which combination of these frozen representations best predicts the target. You skip the expensive part (updating millions of weights) and keep the cheap part (fitting a single linear layer to pre-computed features).

stages.s: Time series: a sequence of values (prices, sensor readings)
Lift with random Fourier features: waves at random frequencies and phases
Run through frozen differential equation: evolve continuously over time
Collect hidden outputs at each time step: fixed representations
Train linear layer on frozen features to predict target

math.words: The output is a linear combination of the frozen model's representations. Each representation is produced by passing lifted features through the differential equation.
symbols: the frozen model's hidden state at time t

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the frozen model outputs a 3-element representation at each time step: h = [2.1, 0.5, 1.8].
To improve the prediction, training nudges W slightly: perhaps W becomes [0.45, 0.25, 0.25].
No weight in the frozen model moves; only W and b change — fast, because there are only 3 numbers to train.

math.note: The entire complexity lives in h_frozen, which is computed once and never retrained. Only the linear combination of these frozen values is learned.

charts.title: Traditional approach: train every weight
charts.note: Expensive to train; requires lots of memory and many passes over the data.

charts.title: Random frozen model: train only readout
charts.note: Dramatically faster; uses far less memory; accuracy is competitive (slight loss is worth the speed-up because training takes 30 times less time, so you can retrain many times on new data or tune its internal settings more often, ultimately winning in real-world deployment).

items.b: The frozen model is too small.
items.html: If the random model does not have enough capacity, even the best readout layer cannot extract good features from it. The random features and differential equation must be large enough to span the space of patterns you need.

items.b: Random features are poorly matched to the data.
items.html: If the Fourier frequencies are chosen badly (all too high or all too low), the lifted input loses important structure before the frozen model even sees it. The choice of random frequencies is a design decision that affects performance.

A single linear layer cannot capture arbitrarily complex nonlinear relationships in the frozen features. If the target depends on complex interactions the readout cannot express, performance will plateau.

items.b: Done right: scale the random model and verify on a validation set.
items.html: Use a large frozen model, tune the Fourier feature frequencies and magnitudes, and measure accuracy on held-out data. A slightly smaller frozen model trained on random features often beats a smaller trainable model.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Implement a random CDE on a standard time-series benchmark (e.g., a currency exchange rate, stock price, or sensor signal). Split the data into train and test. On the training set, freeze the random differential equation and train only the linear readout using linear regression or gradient descent. Measure the mean squared error on the test set and compare it to training a full model with the same architecture using the same time budget. Plot both the prediction and the true signal side by side to see where they diverge.
demo.closing: The frozen model with a trained readout should reach competitive accuracy in a fraction of the training time of a full model.
